opus-5.5.text:
I'd say we're early, but meaningfully past the "toy demo" stage. The honest assessment is that we can do some things reliably today that would have sounded like science fiction a few years ago, and there's still a big gap between where we are and where we want to be.

On the positive side: we can take a model, decompose its internal activations into features that are actually human-interpretable, things like a concept, a style, a behavior, and then intervene on those features directly. We've shown you can steer generation by turning features up or down, and that's not just a parlor trick. It gives you a much more surgical handle than prompting or fine-tuning, because you're editing the mechanism rather than hoping the behavior shifts the way you want. We've also seen real traction on things like identifying and reducing unwanted behaviors, and on understanding *why* a model does something rather than just observing that it does.

Where I'd be careful is in overclaiming. Our decompositions are still imperfect. Features can be messy, they can be polysemantic, and steering can have side effects you didn't anticipate, so you push on one concept and something adjacent moves too. Precision and reliability at scale are the hard problems. Doing a clean edit on one behavior in a controlled setting is very different from saying "we can make a frontier model provably not do X" with high confidence.

So the way I'd frame it is that interpretability has gone from a pure science of understanding to something that's starting to become an engineering discipline. We've got real tools that let people inspect and edit models, and customers and partners are using them. But I think of today as roughly analogous to the early days of a field where the core insight is validated and now the work is making it precise, robust, and general. The trajectory is what excites me. Every time the tools get better, the set of things you can control expands, and I think in a few years intentional design of model behavior, rather than training and hoping, is going to look normal.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say we're honestly still early, but we've come a lot further than I would have guessed a year or two ago. The way I think about it is that there's a spectrum. On one end you have understanding, which is just being able to read what's happening inside a model. On the other end you have control, actually reaching in and changing behavior in a precise, predictable way. And control is the real test, because it's the thing you can't fake. If your explanation of what a feature does is wrong, you find out very fast when you try to steer with it.

Where we are today is that we can reliably find features, in the sparse autoencoder sense, for a huge range of concepts and behaviors in open models. And for a meaningful subset of those, we can steer them and get exactly the behavior change we'd expect, without wrecking the model's overall capabilities. That's the part that's genuinely working. You can dial up or down a tone, a topic, a particular kind of refusal or compliance behavior, and it holds up on held-out prompts.

Where it gets harder is the stuff that really matters for production. First, side effects. A feature is rarely as clean as its label. You push on "formality" and you find you've also nudged verbosity or confidence. Second, composition. Steering one thing is fine, steering five things at once and having them interact well is much harder, and that's what real applications actually want. And third, the gap between editing and fine-tuning. Fine-tuning is still the default tool because it's cheap and people trust it. Our bet is that interpretability-based editing wins on specificity and on being able to say exactly what you changed and why, but we have to keep earning that on real workloads, not just on demos.

So I'd grade us as having real, demonstrable control that's useful in narrow and medium-width cases, and still a ways from the thing we actually want, which is treating a model more like code you can inspect and modify than a black box you can only nudge from the outside. I think that's achievable. I don't think it's achievable by next quarter.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate understanding what’s happening inside a model from being able to reliably change it. Interpretability gives us a way to identify internal features that appear to correspond to concepts or behaviors, and those can become handles for steering the model. But finding a handle isn’t the same as having precise control.

The harder questions are: Does the intervention work across different contexts? Does it change only what you intended? And does it preserve the model’s other capabilities? I think that’s the right bar for assessing our ability to edit models.

So I’d characterize it as promising, but still early. There’s a substantial gap between demonstrating an interesting behavioral change and having a dependable engineering tool. The goal is to close that gap—to make changes that are understandable, targeted, and predictable.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate what we can demonstrate today from what we ultimately want to build. We can identify features inside a model and intervene on them to steer some aspects of its behavior. That’s promising, but it’s different from having precise, reliable control over an entire model.

The hard part is making an edit that does exactly what you intend across different contexts, without changing other things you care about. So I’d describe our current capability as early but meaningful. Interpretability gives us a way to understand and influence what’s happening inside the model; there’s still a lot of work to turn that into dependable editing.
